analysis.one_liner: Ends the overtime pay exemption for commercial truck drivers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after its introduction in September 2022, it was referred to the Senate labor committee and died there when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal wage law has exempted truck drivers from overtime pay since 1938, meaning carriers do not have to pay time-and-a-half when a driver works more than 40 hours in a week. This bill would delete that exemption, so trucking companies would owe overtime to drivers working long weeks. The bill was introduced in the Senate in September 2022 and never moved: it was sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no action before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Commercial truck drivers who work more than 40 hours a week would gain a right to time-and-a-half pay for those extra hours. Long-haul drivers routinely log far more than 40 hours, so the change would directly raise take-home pay for the hours they already work.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Section 13(b)(1) of the Fair Labor Standards Act, the provision that has exempted motor carrier employees from overtime pay since 1938.
After repeal, employers of commercial truck drivers would have to pay overtime to drivers working a workweek longer than 40 hours.

analysis.who_pays: Trucking companies and freight shippers would bear higher labor costs for long workweeks, and some of that cost would likely flow to freight prices. Drivers' schedules are also capped by federal safety rules on driving hours, which limits how much extra time is available at all.

drawbacks.text: Higher overtime costs for carriers would raise freight and shipping costs, which would be passed through to businesses and consumers in the price of goods.

The exemption the bill repeals has existed since 1938 partly because commercial drivers' hours on duty are already capped by separate federal safety rules, so supporters of the status quo argue drivers' total hours are limited in a way other workers' are not.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For drivers who routinely work far beyond 40 hours, mandatory time-and-a-half is a direct and meaningful pay raise for hours already worked, a benefit that would go to a workforce with high turnover and long absences from home. The cost side is real but diffuse: it shows up as slightly higher shipping costs spread across the economy rather than concentrated harm. The bill was narrow and targeted, doing nothing but deleting one exemption, which makes the tradeoff relatively clean.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate's labor committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Padilla introduced the bill on September 13, 2022, joined by four cosponsors: Senators Markey, Sanders, Warren, and Blumenthal.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was taken in the Senate for the remainder of the 117th Congress, and the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Trucking companies keep the 1938-era overtime exemption, so they continue to pay straight time for hours beyond 40 that many drivers routinely work. Drivers gain nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Trucking companies that avoid overtime costs

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists; its sponsor and all four cosponsors were Democrats or independents, and no Republican publicly supported it in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the industry's 1938-era exemption from overtime pay, requiring time-and-a-half for driver workweeks over 40 hours. That exemption is worth a share of driver labor costs to carriers, so its loss would raise operating expenses.
Higher carrier labor costs would likely pass through as higher freight rates. The effect would be modest and spread across the economy.
